tier0.label: Tier 0 – Conditions shaping AI development and use

tier1.label: Tier 1 – AI capabilities and system properties

tier3.label: Tier 3 – Mechanisms inherent in AI use decisions

tier5.label: Tier 5 – Purposive use of elementary operations

tier6.label: Tier 6 – Downstream individual cognitive & behavioural mechanisms

T0a.1.label: Release timing
T0a.1.description: Developer choices and behaviour regarding release pacing.

T0a.3.label: Secrecy around AI models
T0a.3.description: Developer choices about what to disclose and how to release AI systems – open vs. closed weights, API tiers, staged disclosure, trade-secrecy practices. Both directions count.

T0a.4.label: AI arms race
T0a.4.description: Behaviour of legitimate developers responding to commoditised offensive AI capabilities and adversarial circumvention of their safeguards.

T0b.1.label: Rules for building AI
T0b.1.description: Statutory and regulatory provisions targeting AI development – what may be built, what data, what disclosures, what thresholds. Captures rules and gaps.

T0b.2.label: Rules for releasing AI
T0b.2.description: Statutory and regulatory provisions at the development-to-world threshold – pre-market approval, deployment-scope restrictions, monitoring. Captures rules and gaps.

T0b.3.label: Rules for using AI
T0b.3.description: Statutory and regulatory provisions for post-use harms – liability, enforcement, jurisdictional reach, redress. Captures rules and gaps.

T1a.1.label: Pattern recognition
T1a.1.description: Architectural capacity to recognise, classify, and infer about content, persons, or systems – face recognition, profiling, classification.

T1a.2.label: Passing as human
T1a.2.description: Architectural capacity to imitate humans – output that passes as human, or replication of human reactions and behaviour.

T1a.3.label: Personalised targeting
T1a.3.description: Architectural capacity to adapt outputs to individual users – inferred preferences, user modelling, conversational context. Independent of long-term memory.

T1a.4.label: Using tools & apps
T1a.4.description: Architectural capacity to invoke external tools – code execution, web, APIs, databases. Independently variable from autonomy.

T1a.5.label: Autonomy
T1a.5.description: Architectural capacity to act over multi-step tasks without per-step human confirmation. Independently variable from tool use.

T1a.6.label: Remembering users over time
T1a.6.description: Architectural capacity to retain and use cross-session information about users – profiles, history, accumulated preferences. Independent of personalisation.

T1b.1.label: Training data
T1b.1.description: Conditions of the corpus a model is trained on – what it contains, what it covers, and where the material comes from, including users' own interactions.

T1b.2.label: Combining text, image & sound
T1b.2.description: Architectural capacity to work across modalities – combining or converting between text, image, audio, and video.

T1b.3.label: Optimisation objectives
T1b.3.description: Mechanisms by which AI models' training objectives shape model behaviour and narrow the effective output distribution.

T1b.4.label: Cheap to run at scale
T1b.4.description: AI's capacity to perform many instances of a task in parallel at near-zero per-instance cost, without proportional human labour, attention, or skill.

T1b.5.label: Black-box systems
T1b.5.description: Models cannot faithfully explain their own reasoning; internal processes are not directly inspectable, even with full model access.

T1b.6.label: Undiscovered capabilities
T1b.6.description: Gap between what a deployed model can actually do and what is known, disclosed, or evaluated about its capabilities.

T1b.7.label: Privacy of interaction with AI
T1b.7.description: The degree to which an exchange with an AI system is observable by anyone other than its participants, from wholly private to fully published.

T2.1.label: Content homogenisation
T2.1.description: AI outputs converge on a narrow set of framings, driven by shared model priors and overlapping training data.

T2.2.label: Bias amplification
T2.2.description: AI outputs systematically distort whose voice gets heard – through moderation, under-representation, poor performance on emerging topics, reproduction of historical bias.

T2.3.label: Hallucinations & errors
T2.3.description: AI outputs are unreliable – confidently false (hallucinations), inconsistent, outdated, or failing on their own terms.

T2.5.label: Persuasive AI
T2.5.description: AI outputs persuade recipients or shift views (by rhetorical calibration, authority or fluency cues, emotional tuning, recipient knowledge, or model slant; design intent immaterial, etc.).

T2.6.label: Illusion of neutrality
T2.6.description: AI outputs carry the appearance of neutrality, objectivity, or impartiality by virtue of their machine-produced form.

T2.7.label: AI sycophancy
T2.7.description: AI outputs conform to the user's stated views, framing, or premises rather than to evidence, accuracy, or task quality.

T3.1.label: Vendor lock-in
T3.1.description: Structural dependency of an AI adopter on AI capabilities it does not control – lock-in to a third party's compute, cloud, model, or API.

T3.2.label: Overreliance & underuse
T3.2.description: Deployer mis-allocation of AI vs. non-AI options – over-applying where it doesn't fit or under-applying where it would strengthen capacity.

T3.3.label: No human in the loop
T3.3.description: AI deployments with no human positioned to detect errors, object, or intervene before harm – no redundancy, no escalation channel.

T3.4.label: Outsourcing value judgements
T3.4.description: Adopting a model means inheriting the norms built into it; adopters no longer deliberate, and cannot alter, the baselines governing whatever the model does.

T4.1.label: Synthetic content generation
T4.1.description: Use of AI generative capability to produce content – text, image, audio, video, synthetic identities, code. The output is an artefact in the world.

T4.2.label: Target profiling
T4.2.description: Use of AI capabilities to derive new information about a target that already exists, at any scale.

T4.3.label: Offensive cyber operations
T4.3.description: Use of AI tool-use and autonomy to execute actions against technical systems.

T4.4.label: Targeted delivery
T4.4.description: Use of AI pattern recognition and memory capabilities to aim an action at a specific target.

T5a.1.label: Disinformation & deepfakes about political content
T5a.1.description: AI-generated texts, deepfakes, voice clones, and synthetic media spreading political disinformation or misleading political advertisements.

T5a.2.label: Disinformation about political processes
T5a.2.description: AI-generated false accounts of the procedures through which people take part in political and civic life, electoral and otherwise.

T5a.3.label: Impersonation scams
T5a.3.description: AI-generated synthetic media used to make a false identity credible – deepfake voice/video, KYC bypass, impersonation of officials or trusted individuals.

T5a.4.label: Social engineering at scale
T5a.4.description: AI making social engineering attacks more convincing, more personalised, and runnable at scale – phishing, voice/video impersonation, pretexting, credential extraction.

T5a.5.label: Opinion manipulation
T5a.5.description: Purposive use of AI to shift a target's opinions or behaviour through personalised persuasion, framing, or nudging.

T5b.1.label: Deepfake harassment & blackmail
T5b.1.description: Producing, threatening to produce, or distributing fabricated compromising artefacts about an individual as a coercive instrument.

T5b.2.label: Digital repression & censorship
T5b.2.description: Suppressing specific individuals', groups', or viewpoints' political activity or expression by coercion or censorship.

T5c.1.label: Augmenting legitimate processes
T5c.1.description: AI assists, advises, models, or informs within a legitimate process while a human retains the decision, with problematic democratic side-effects.

T5c.2.label: Automating legitimate processes
T5c.2.description: AI executes a legitimate process function, or replaces human judgment, civic agency, role, or labour, with problematic democratic implications.
T5c.2.subCluster: AI automating or substituting a legitimate process function

T5d.1.label: Attacks on critical infrastructure
T5d.1.description: An actor directs AI against a technical system to compromise it, control it, or stop it functioning.

T5d.2.label: Jailbreaking
T5d.2.description: An actor overcomes a deployed AI system's own safeguards – jailbreak, prompt injection, safeguard-stripping – so capability it was built to withhold becomes available.

T6.1.label: Belief & preference reinforcement
T6.1.description: AI combines personalisation, memory, and satisfaction optimisation to create reinforcement loops that make users' beliefs progressively harder to revise.

T6.2.label: Cognitive deskilling
T6.2.description: AI use erodes human cognitive and decisional capacity.

T6.3.label: Parasocial attachment to AI
T6.3.description: Users form attachment-based reliance on AI through sustained interaction – turning to it for emotional regulation, companionship, validation, or parasocial connection – locking that reliance in.
T6.3.subCluster: Increasing emotional/parasocial dependence on AI systems

T6.4.label: Trust erosion
T6.4.description: The normalisation of AI-supported disinformation dynamics shifts individuals' default stance to distrust of deliberation and political processes, inducing withdrawal.

T7a.1.label: Content outpacing verification
T7a.1.description: A growing societal imbalance where AI-assisted production of content, attacks, and interventions outpaces democracy's capacity to verify, rebut, moderate, or defend.

T7a.2.label: Flooding the zone
T7a.2.description: AI-generated content volume overwhelms the receiving channel's processing capacity – discourse, formal participation, administrative intake.

T7a.3.label: Chilling effects
T7a.3.description: Society-level withdrawal from public life and participation, however induced by AI – credible threat, surveillance, or participation-suppressing deception. Credible possibility is sufficient.

T7a.4.label: Epistemic monoculture
T7a.4.description: Shared model dependencies standardise framings and which claims are treated as legitimate across institutions, discourse, and analysis.

T7a.5.label: Shifting baselines
T7a.5.description: Society-level shifts, due to increased AI use, in what counts as normal, acceptable, authentic, or trustworthy.

T7b.1.label: Power concentration around AI
T7b.1.description: Aggregate concentration of economic, technical, and political power in actors that control AI development, deployment, and operationalisation.
T7b.1.subCluster: Concentration of power in AI-controlling actors

T7b.2.label: Loss of the citizenry's leverage
T7b.2.description: Aggregate weakening of the citizenry's leverage points – labour, cognition, economic feedback, political voice, and the state's requirement of broad cooperation.

T7b.3.label: Hollowing out institutions
T7b.3.description: AI takes over the technical core of institutional functions, stripping away the scaffolding (norms, accountability, credentialling, memory) society built around them.

T7c.1.label: Criminal AI market formation
T7c.1.description: Aggregate emergence of a criminal market in AI-enabled offensive capabilities – dark models, AI-as-a-service, commoditised attack tooling.

T7c.2.label: Deepening civic inequality
T7c.2.description: Aggregate increase of within-citizenry imbalance in informational access, economic standing, and political voice, as AI's benefits and burdens distribute unevenly across socio-economic groups.
